summary: A 1943 Ottawa Journal account, reproduced on Canada Lookouts, describes a 30.5 m steel lookout above Ivanhoe Lake near Foleyet, worked by a woman lookout; no fate found.

facts.design: Steel girders carrying an eight-foot square cab

events.note: Mrs. Raoul Languerand worked the tower seven days a week, as the October 1943 Ottawa Journal reported; the paper called her the only woman lookout in the Ontario Forestry Service.

evidence.supports: Cab sits atop 100-foot steel girders, 1,200 feet above Ivanhoe Lake
evidence.quote: atop 100-foot high steel girders and 1,200 feet above Ivanhoe Lake

evidence.supports: Name comes from a wild township on the timber map
evidence.quote: called Hellyer Tower after the wild township on the timber map

evidence.supports: Lookout was a woman, the only one in the Ontario Forestry Service
evidence.quote: The only woman lookout in the Ontario Forestry Service

evidence.supports: Worked seven days a week, most of the working day in the glassed-in tower
evidence.quote: she spends most of her working day, seven days a week

evidence.supports: Climbed the 100 rungs at least three times a day, usually five
evidence.quote: she climbs the 100 rungs to the tower top at least three times a day and usually five

evidence.supports: Home was a small white cabin at the base, reached by a rough trail of over a mile and a half
evidence.quote: is a small white cabin at the base of the tower and is reached by hiking over a mile and a half-long rough trail from the lakeshore to the summit

evidence.supports: Lake name changed to Ivanhoe Lake in 1960 according to the Foleyet article
evidence.quote: It was only in 1960 that Lake Pishkanogami became Ivanhoe Lake or lac Ivanhoe in French.

notes_for_editor: The description, staffing and cab size rest on one 1943 Ottawa Journal article, which the Canada Lookouts page reproduces; the original newspaper was not read, and the reproduction is a fan site. No construction year, builder, fate or present state was found in any source read. Search results for Languerand returned a genealogy site, which was not used. Name conflict: the 1943 article calls the water Ivanhoe Lake, but the Foleyet article says Lake Pishkanogami became Ivanhoe Lake only in 1960; the story keeps the 1943 wording and flags the clash. The 100-foot figure is the height of the steel girders in the article, so height_m 30.5 may differ from the full structure height. The trail is 'over a mile and a half' in the article, and the story says the same. The record coordinates (48.16446, -82.49721) were not checked against any text. The agency fact rests only on the article naming that service as the lookout's employer.
